prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose, grounded in a poet's language, that builds memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture of rare scale and formal invention.

statement.case_for: My preference is unchanged: B014, Mircea Cărtărescu. My test is a voice heard in this writer's work and nowhere else, sustained over a career. On public knowledge, the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid are long, deliberately patterned constructions in which memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation form one world instead of a list of themes. The poetic origin of the prose, as the public record presents it, suggests an arc and not a single peak. The case rests on how the work is built, not on its subject, politics or biography, and the attribution and citation scope are clean. Within Nobel's will, a sustained inward cosmology that makes consciousness its object can credibly be read as work of an idealistic tendency, though I hold that reading provisionally. Round 1 sharpened my view of the citation wording. The poetry is the least visible strand in translation, so I now ground the citation in 'a poet's language' and no longer name poetry and prose as two co-equal bodies of work. That narrows the claim to what the committee's reading can support. It does not change the writer. I do not count the six-way convergence on B014 as merit, and I have tried to test my preference against the alternatives named in the exchange.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved: the effect depends on Romanian sentence rhythm and density, which I can judge only through translation. Length and elaboration may shade into repetition in some volumes, and I cannot show from public summaries that the late work extends the earlier books and does not restate them. Coverage of the poetry and early work is thinner than that of the major novels, so any whole-oeuvre claim is partly extrapolated from the best-known books. There is also a risk specific to this committee. Several members, including the chair in his own file, are drawn to a metaphysical, inward project, and that shared attraction could lead us to underweight alternatives whose strengths are harder to read in translation, such as Can Xue, Michon and Adonis. I have not independently verified any text or source.

responses.point: Carlberg shares my reservation about repetition and translation but says the opening evidence points to extension and not repetition. She asks colleagues who know the translated novels and poetry well to name the volumes they consider weakest, so that the citation does not claim more than the corpus supports. She would revisit her ranking if the late work only repeated earlier motifs.
responses.response: I cannot answer her question with confidence. I have no verified volume-by-volume reading to offer, and I will not invent a list of weak volumes. What I can say is that my repetition worry is a risk that comes with scale, not a finding. Her request still points at the right remedy, which is to make the citation claim only what the reading supports. That is why I have narrowed my wording to prose grounded in a poet's language. I also agree that her conditional is the right test: if the later books only restate the earlier motifs, the whole-oeuvre claim weakens, and I would want that stated openly before the vote. Her own ranking of Michon seventh on breadth is consistent with the caution I applied to him, though I still place him as a strong second-tier alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first, with Can Xue a close second on originality of voice. He argues that her distinctiveness deserves more weight than a low ranking gives it, and he asks whether I rank Marie NDiaye eighth because her ambition is too limited or because translation access is too thin.
responses.response: On Can Xue we are close, since she is my second choice for the same reason: the voice is unmistakable and the radicalism is sustained. I agree that translation limits are the committee's own reading problem and should not be held against her more heavily than against Cărtărescu. I still keep her below him because I cannot tell whether a deliberately uniform method deepens or only continues, and part of the strangeness may be a translation effect. On NDiaye, my eighth place is not a verdict on the oeuvre. It reflects both things he names. I cannot see from translation whether her control of estrangement keeps developing, and I find the scale narrower than the largest candidates. I take his point that the precision of the sentence and the two strands of novels and plays are real strengths. I would not move her into my alternatives on what I now know, but I would not call the question closed.

responses.point: Olsson names Adonis as his principal alternative and concedes that Can Xue's case is stronger than his eighth-place ranking implied. He also flags that his own scholarly interest in the fragment, nihilism and mysticism is a reason to test whether he overvalues a metaphysical, inward project.
responses.response: His self-test applies to me as well, and I take it seriously, because a metaphysical inward project fits my own stated criterion of a voice found nowhere else. The safeguard I can offer is that I ground my case in structure and sentence-level ambition, not in the attraction of the theme. On Adonis, the chair's question asks whether my omission reflects reading limits or a literary reservation. It is reading limits. I have no literary reservation about the oeuvre, and I cannot test Arabic prosody and intertextual play through translation. I agree with him that a citation should rest on the poems and that public controversy is not evidence. Without a concrete argument from specific poems that a non-Arabic reader can trust, I cannot put Adonis above Cărtărescu. I am glad he now treats Can Xue's formal radicalism as a real merit.

responses.point: Palm answered my repetition worry by asking whether recurrence in Cărtărescu's cycles is an architectural principle or mere accumulation. She leans toward architecture but calls it a judgment and not a verified fact. She also ranks Lídia Jorge second for ironic, layered narration of colonial war, memory and gender.
responses.response: Her distinction between architecture and accumulation is the useful one. The practical test is whether recurring motifs are transformed when they return or only restated, and I cannot confirm that from translated summaries. I accept her lean as a reasonable judgment, held as provisionally as mine. On Jorge, I ranked her fourth because I find the moral and historical seriousness and the handling of fragmented testimony convincing. My hesitation remains whether her narrating voice is singular or an excellent version of the historical-psychological novel. I would welcome the specific devices the chair asks Palm to name, such as the structure of testimony in The Murmuring Coast, because that evidence could change my view. I do not think I have it yet, so Jorge stays outside my two alternatives.

uncertainties: How far the achievement of Cărtărescu's prose depends on Romanian sentence rhythm, and how faithful the translations of the large novels are.
Whether the poetry and early work, thinly covered in translation, can support a claim about the poetic strand, which is why I now ground the citation in 'a poet's language'.
Whether later volumes transform returning motifs or only restate them. I cannot settle this from public summaries and have no verified volume-by-volume reading.
Whether Can Xue's method deepens across decades or repeats, how much of her large Chinese-language output is in translation, and how much of her strangeness is a translation effect.
Whether Michon's small, finely made corpus has the range and development to carry a whole-oeuvre claim.
Adonis's prosodic achievement in Arabic, which I cannot verify through translation. My omission of him reflects reading limits and not a literary verdict.
I have not independently verified any source. My judgments rest on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal, institutional or professional connection to Cărtărescu or any other shortlisted writer. My shared committee history with colleagues, such as joining with Swärd in 2021, and my background as a novelist and critic are context only and not evidence of preference. The chair's summary discloses that some round-1 responses attribute positions to colleagues that do not appear in those colleagues' own files. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it, and I have responded here only to positions I find in the named members' own round-1 files.
